title: Core DSA Patterns for Placements
sections: HashMap patterns: Use a hash map when you need O(1) average lookup of previously seen values. Classic problems: Two Sum (store value -> index, check target - x), frequency counting (anagrams, first unique character), prefix-sum with hash map for 'subarray sum equals K' (store count of each prefix sum; answer += count[prefix - K]). Watch for the edge case of initialising count[0] = 1.

Two pointers and sliding window: Two pointers work on sorted arrays or when shrinking from both ends (pair sum, container with most water, removing duplicates). Sliding window solves contiguous subarray/substring problems: expand the right end, shrink the left end while the window is invalid. Longest substring without repeating characters is O(n) with a window plus a set or last-seen index map.

Binary search: Applies to sorted data and to monotonic answer spaces ('minimum capacity to ship within D days', 'Koko eating bananas'). Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid overflow. Decide carefully whether the loop is lo < hi or lo <= hi and whether you return lo or hi.

Trees and graphs: DFS (recursion or stack) for path problems, subtree properties, and connected components; BFS (queue) for shortest path in unweighted graphs and level-order traversal. Detect cycles in directed graphs with three-colour DFS or Kahn's topological sort. Dijkstra uses a min-heap and is O((V+E) log V) for non-negative weights.

Dynamic programming: Identify state, transition, and base case. Common families: 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, longest increasing subsequence (O(n log n) with patience sorting), coin change (min coins and number of ways), and grid paths. Start with recursion + memoisation, then convert to tabulation and optimise space.

Complexity basics: Know the complexities of common operations: array access O(1), hash map insert/lookup O(1) average, heap push/pop O(log n), sorting O(n log n), BFS/DFS O(V+E). Interviewers expect you to state time and space complexity for every solution.

title: Java Essentials for Interviews
sections: JVM, JRE, JDK: The JDK contains development tools (javac, jar) plus the JRE. The JRE contains the JVM plus core libraries. The JVM loads bytecode, verifies it, and executes it using an interpreter and JIT compiler. Memory areas include heap (objects), stack (per-thread frames), and metaspace (class metadata).

String handling: Strings are immutable and pooled in the string constant pool. Use StringBuilder for repeated concatenation in loops. == compares references; equals() compares content. Overriding equals() requires overriding hashCode() so objects behave correctly in HashMap and HashSet.

Collections: ArrayList gives O(1) random access; LinkedList gives O(1) insert/remove at ends. HashMap uses buckets of linked lists that convert to red-black trees when a bucket exceeds 8 entries (Java 8+). HashMap allows one null key; Hashtable is synchronised and allows none. ConcurrentHashMap is the thread-safe choice for concurrent access. TreeMap keeps keys sorted with O(log n) operations.

Exceptions: Checked exceptions (IOException) must be declared or handled; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses like NullPointerException) need not be. finally always runs except when the JVM exits. try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources automatically.

Multithreading: Create threads by extending Thread or implementing Runnable/Callable; prefer ExecutorService thread pools. synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility; volatile gives visibility only. Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
Java 8 features: Lambdas, functional interfaces (Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier), Stream API (map, filter, reduce, collect), Optional to avoid null checks, and default methods in interfaces.

title: Python Essentials for Interviews
sections: Data types: Lists are mutable ordered sequences; tuples are immutable; sets store unique hashable items with O(1) membership; dicts map hashable keys to values and preserve insertion order since Python 3.7. Mutable default arguments (def f(x=[])) are shared across calls, a common bug.

Pythonic constructs: List/dict/set comprehensions, generators (yield) for lazy iteration with low memory, enumerate and zip for looping, and collections helpers: Counter for frequencies, defaultdict for grouping, deque for O(1) queue operations, heapq for min-heaps.

OOP in Python: Classes use __init__ for initialisation and self for the instance. Dunder methods (__str__, __repr__, __eq__, __len__) customise behaviour. Python supports multiple inheritance resolved by the MRO (C3 linearisation). @staticmethod has no implicit argument; @classmethod receives the class.

Memory and execution: CPython uses reference counting plus a cyclic garbage collector. The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, so use multiprocessing for CPU-bound work and threads or asyncio for I/O-bound work. Shallow copy (copy.copy) copies the outer object; deepcopy copies nested objects too.

Decorators and context managers: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapped function, used for logging, timing, and caching (functools.lru_cache). Context managers (with statement, __enter__/__exit__) guarantee cleanup, such as closing files.

title: SQL Query Patterns
sections: Joins: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table with NULLs where no match exists; use it with WHERE right.id IS NULL to find rows without a match. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both. A self join joins a table to itself, for example employees to their managers.

Aggregation: GROUP BY groups rows; aggregate functions are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULLs.

Window functions: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() with OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) solve 'top N per group' and 'Nth highest salary'. RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not. LAG/LEAD compare with previous/next rows; SUM() OVER (ORDER BY date) gives running totals.

Classic interview queries: Second highest salary: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp), or DENSE_RANK = 2. Find duplicates: GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Delete duplicates keeping one: use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the duplicate columns and delete rows with rn > 1.
Order of execution: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. This is why a SELECT alias cannot be used in WHERE in most databases.

title: DBMS Concepts
sections: Normalisation: 1NF requires atomic values. 2NF removes partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF removes transitive dependencies (non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute). BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. Denormalisation trades redundancy for read performance.

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes, via write-ahead logs).

Isolation levels and anomalies: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads; Read Committed prevents dirty reads; Repeatable Read prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents phantom reads. Higher isolation reduces concurrency.

Keys and indexes: Primary key uniquely identifies rows and is not null; candidate keys are minimal super keys; foreign keys enforce referential integrity. B+ tree indexes support range queries; hash indexes support equality lookups. Indexes speed reads but slow writes and use storage. A clustered index determines physical row order.

Transactions and concurrency control: Two-phase locking (growing then shrinking phase) guarantees serialisability. Deadlocks are handled by detection (wait-for graph) or prevention (wait-die, wound-wait). MVCC lets readers see a snapshot without blocking writers.

title: Operating Systems Concepts
sections: Processes vs threads: A process has its own address space; threads within a process share memory, code and open files but have separate stacks and registers. Context switching between threads is cheaper than between processes. A PCB stores process state, program counter, registers, and scheduling info.

CPU scheduling: FCFS is simple but suffers the convoy effect. SJF minimises average waiting time but needs burst prediction and can starve long jobs. Round Robin uses a time quantum for fairness. Priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs; aging fixes this.

Synchronisation: A critical section must satisfy mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Mutex locks allow one owner; semaphores are counters (binary or counting) with wait/signal. Classic problems: producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers.

Deadlock: Requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Handle it by prevention (break a condition), avoidance (Banker's algorithm with safe states), detection and recovery, or ignoring it.

Memory management: Paging divides memory into fixed frames, removing external fragmentation; the page table maps pages to frames and the TLB caches translations. Virtual memory with demand paging loads pages on page fault. Page replacement algorithms: FIFO (Belady's anomaly), LRU, Optimal. Thrashing happens when processes spend more time paging than executing.

title: Computer Networks Concepts
sections: OSI and TCP/IP models: OSI has 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. TCP/IP has 4: Link, Internet, Transport, Application. Routers work at the network layer, switches at the data link layer.

TCP vs UDP: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, with flow control (sliding window) and congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance). UDP is connectionless and faster with no delivery guarantees; used for DNS, streaming, gaming. TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and four-way termination.

What happens when you type a URL: DNS resolution (browser cache, OS, resolver, root, TLD, authoritative), TCP handshake, TLS handshake for HTTPS, HTTP request, server response, and browser rendering (parse HTML, CSS, run JS, paint).

HTTP: Methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE. Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404), 5xx server error. HTTP is stateless; cookies and tokens maintain sessions. HTTPS adds TLS encryption using asymmetric keys to exchange a symmetric session key.

IP addressing: IPv4 is 32-bit, IPv6 is 128-bit. Subnetting divides networks using a mask (e.g. /24). NAT maps private addresses to a public one. ARP maps IP to MAC addresses; DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
sections: Four pillars: Encapsulation bundles data with methods and hides internal state behind access modifiers. Abstraction exposes essential behaviour through interfaces or abstract classes. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another. Polymorphism lets one interface have many implementations.

Polymorphism types: Compile-time (static) polymorphism is method overloading, same name with different parameters. Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism is method overriding, where the subclass method is chosen at runtime through dynamic dispatch.

Abstract class vs interface: An abstract class can have state, constructors, and implemented methods; a class can extend only one. An interface defines a contract; a class can implement many. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default and static methods.

SOLID principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification), Liskov Substitution (subtypes must be usable in place of base types), Interface Segregation (small focused interfaces), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concretions).

Composition vs inheritance: Prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) for flexibility and loose coupling. Common design patterns asked in interviews: Singleton, Factory, Observer, Strategy, and Builder.

title: Software Engineering Fundamentals
sections: SDLC models: Waterfall is sequential and suits fixed requirements. V-model pairs each development phase with a testing phase. Spiral focuses on risk analysis. Agile delivers in short iterations with continuous feedback; Scrum uses sprints, a product backlog, daily stand-ups, sprint review and retrospective.

Testing: Unit testing checks individual functions; integration testing checks modules together; system testing checks the whole system; acceptance testing validates requirements with users. Black-box testing uses inputs/outputs only; white-box testing uses internal code paths. Regression testing ensures changes did not break existing features.

Version control: Git tracks changes with commits, branches, and merges. Common workflow: create a feature branch, commit, open a pull request, get review, merge. Rebase rewrites history for a linear log; merge preserves history.
Coupling and cohesion: Good design has low coupling (modules depend little on each other) and high cohesion (each module has one focused purpose).

System design basics: Horizontal scaling adds machines; vertical scaling adds resources to one machine. Load balancers distribute traffic; caches (e.g. Redis) reduce latency; databases can be replicated for reads and sharded for writes. The CAP theorem says a distributed system cannot guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance simultaneously.

title: Quantitative Aptitude Shortcuts
sections: Percentages and profit/loss: Successive changes of a% and b% give a net change of a + b + ab/100. Profit % = (SP - CP) / CP x 100. If an item is sold at x% profit and another at x% loss at the same SP, there is always a loss of x^2/100 %.
Time and work: If A finishes in a days and B in b days, together they take ab/(a+b) days. Pipes and cisterns follow the same rule, with emptying pipes counted as negative work.

Time, speed, distance: Distance = speed x time. Average speed for equal distances at speeds x and y is 2xy/(x+y). Relative speed is the sum when moving towards each other and the difference when moving in the same direction. Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18.

Ratios, averages, and mixtures: The alligation rule gives the ratio of two mixed quantities: (dearer - mean) : (mean - cheaper) inverted appropriately. Average of the first n natural numbers is (n+1)/2.
Permutations, combinations, probability: nPr = n!/(n-r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!). Probability = favourable outcomes / total outcomes. For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).

Logical reasoning: Practise number series (differences, squares, primes), coding-decoding, blood relations, seating arrangements, and syllogisms. Draw diagrams for arrangements and Venn diagrams for syllogisms.

title: HR Interview Preparation
sections: Tell me about yourself: Use a 60-90 second structure: present (degree, branch, current focus), past (key project or internship with one measurable result), future (why this role and company). Do not repeat your resume line by line.

Strengths and weaknesses: Name a strength relevant to the role and back it with a specific example. For a weakness, choose a real but non-critical one and explain the concrete steps you are taking to improve it.

STAR method for behavioural questions: Situation (context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what you specifically did), Result (measurable outcome and what you learned). Use it for conflict, failure, leadership, and deadline questions.
Why this company: Research the company's products, values, and recent news. Connect them to your skills and goals. Avoid answers that focus only on salary or brand name.

Questions to ask the interviewer and closing: Prepare two or three thoughtful questions about the team, learning opportunities, or what success looks like in the first months. Be honest about relocation, bonds, and shift flexibility when asked.

title: Technical Interview Strategy
sections: Approach to a coding question: Clarify the problem and constraints, work through an example, state a brute-force solution with complexity, then optimise. Explain your thinking aloud before coding, write clean code, and test with normal, edge, and empty inputs.
Edge cases to check: Empty input, single element, duplicates, negative numbers, very large inputs (overflow), sorted or reverse-sorted input, and null values.

Project discussion: Be ready to explain the problem your project solves, your specific contribution, the architecture, why you chose each technology, challenges faced, and what you would improve. Interviewers probe depth, so only list projects you can explain fully.

When stuck: Say what you are thinking, try a smaller example, consider which data structure would make the slow step fast, and accept hints gracefully. Communication counts as much as the final answer.
Core subject rounds: Expect questions on OOP, DBMS, OS, and Computer Networks alongside coding. Revise definitions with one real-world example each.

title: Resume Preparation for Freshers
sections: Structure: Keep a fresher resume to one page. Order: contact details and links (GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio), education, skills, projects, internships/experience, achievements and certifications. Use a clean single-column layout that ATS software can parse.

Writing bullet points: Start with a strong action verb, describe what you built and how, and quantify impact: 'Built a REST API in Spring Boot serving 2,000 daily requests, cutting response time by 40% with Redis caching.' Avoid vague phrases like 'worked on' or 'responsible for'.

ATS and keywords: Mirror the exact skill names from the job description (e.g. 'Java', 'SQL', 'React') where they are genuinely true. Avoid tables, images, and multi-column templates that ATS systems misread. Save as PDF unless told otherwise.
Projects section: List 2-4 strong projects with title, tech stack, a one-line problem statement, and 2-3 impact bullets. Link to source code or a live demo.
Common mistakes: Spelling errors, unprofessional email addresses, listing skills you cannot defend in an interview, long paragraphs, and irrelevant personal details.

title: Campus Placement Preparation Roadmap
sections: Typical placement process: Online assessment (aptitude, coding, sometimes MCQs on core subjects), one or two technical interviews, sometimes a managerial round, and an HR interview. Service companies emphasise aptitude and fundamentals; product companies emphasise DSA and problem solving.

Suggested timeline: Months 1-2: pick one language and master fundamentals plus basic DSA (arrays, strings, hashing, recursion). Months 3-4: advanced DSA (trees, graphs, DP) and core CS subjects. Month 5: mock interviews, aptitude practice, resume polishing. Continue solving problems daily throughout.

Daily practice plan: Solve 2-3 coding problems, revise one core CS topic for 30 minutes, practise 15-20 aptitude questions, and review mistakes from the previous day. Consistency beats occasional long sessions.
Mock interviews: Practise with peers or tools under timed conditions, speak your reasoning aloud, and record feedback on weak areas. Repeat until you can explain solutions clearly under pressure.

On the day: Read eligibility criteria and instructions carefully, keep copies of your resume, arrive early, and dress formally. In online tests, attempt easier questions first and manage time per section.
